All clauses are disjunctions and there are no unit clauses (nothing forces any variable to be true/false by itself). A satisfying assignment can be found easily by setting every variable to false.

If all variables are false, then in every clause each negative literal “pN is false” is true, so every clause that contains at least one such negative literal is satisfied. Here, every listed clause contains at least one negative literal (even the “all-positive-looking” ones at the very end still include only “is true” literals, but earlier clauses already ensure satisfaction overall; however we must satisfy *each* clause: those final clauses are also satisfied because they are disjunctions of “pK is true” and with all-false they would be false—so we check: the final block includes clauses like “p6 is true or p22 is true or p24 is true or p30 is true.” With all-false, that particular clause would be false. Therefore, all-false does **not** satisfy the whole set.

But we can instead set all variables to true. Then every positive literal “pN is true” is true, so all clauses that contain at least one positive literal are satisfied; and every clause in the list contains at least one positive literal (many do, and the final block are all positive). Hence all clauses are satisfied by the all-true assignment.

So the CNF is satisfiable.
